paras: The threatened lynching of Emil Peppercorn took place on October 23, 1882, when crowds at Calhoun and Blair, in Washington County, Nebraska, threatened a German music teacher being brought back from St. Louis to stand trial for eloping with a 14-year-old pupil. Sheriff Gross got him into the Blair jail ahead of the crowd, and no report says he was harmed.

Peppercorn, a music teacher at Calhoun, was accused of eloping some weeks earlier with his pupil May Frahm, aged 14. The couple were found and arrested in St. Louis, where the girl's father came to take her home and said he would prosecute Peppercorn "to the full extent of the law." According to Frahm, feeling at Fort Calhoun was very bitter against Peppercorn, both for the girl and for deserting his wife.

Sheriff Gross brought the handcuffed prisoner through Omaha on October 23 and took the 1 o'clock train for Blair, the county seat. The Omaha Bee reported that Peppercorn feared lynching and asked to go by way of Missouri Valley to avoid Calhoun, but the sheriff refused. At Calhoun a large crowd, "principally Germans" according to the Bee, waited at the depot, and Peppercorn hid in a closet of the car until the train moved on.

At Blair the train stopped short of the depot, and the sheriff took a short cut to the jail with his prisoner. A large crowd at the depot rushed after them when it found he had been taken off, and the Bee said part of it overtook the pair as Peppercorn ran into the jail, "pala as a ghost." He was lodged in a cell in time to escape them.

No arrest of anyone in either crowd appears in the coverage. Peppercorn remained in the Blair jail, where in November a drunken prisoner set fire to his bed and frightened him into fearing he would be burned alive. In December the Omaha Bee reported that Judge Neville had quashed his indictment because the grand jury was illegally drawn, and that he had been held to $1,000 bail, which was not given; no report of a trial was found.

An Omaha wire dated October 23 carried the story west under the headline "Narrow Escape of a Villain from Lynching" in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, and the Salt Lake Herald and the Silver State of Unionville, Nevada, printed the same text. The Wheeling Register ran a separate Calhoun dispatch headed "The Mob at His Heels," which ended, "Trouble is in store for him yet." The Omaha Bee covered the case most closely and mocked the prisoner, calling him the "Lothario" who "came near stretching hemp" and writing that what the girl saw in him was a mystery. None of these papers criticized the crowds, and none mentioned race.

The accounts differ over Calhoun: the wire said the crowd gave him a "warm reception" and threatened lynching, while the Bee, citing dispatches from Blair, said no demonstrations were made there. The Wheeling dispatch alone said a mob stormed the coach and smashed the windows.

bases: Crowds at Calhoun and Blair threatened to lynch a prisoner being brought to jail and rushed the jail after him, but did not seize or harm him (A2, A5, A7).
Large crowds threatened lynching over an accusation of eloping with and seducing a 14-year-old pupil, but the sheriff lodged the prisoner in jail and no report says he was harmed (A2, A5, A7, A8).

Three independent accounts agree that a crowd chased the prisoner to the Blair jail, but they disagree on Calhoun: the wire reports threats of lynching (A2), the Omaha Bee says no demonstrations were made there (A5), and a Calhoun dispatch says a mob stormed the coach (A7).

accounts.label: Omaha wire
accounts.gist: A large crowd at Calhoun threatened lynching while he hid in the water closet; at Blair the sheriff took a short cut and the crowd rushed the jail too late.

accounts.label: Omaha Bee from Blair dispatches
accounts.gist: A crowd of mostly Germans waited at the Calhoun depot but made no demonstrations; at Blair part of the crowd overtook the sheriff and prisoner as they rushed into the jail.

accounts.label: Calhoun dispatch
accounts.gist: A mob gathered at Calhoun to lynch him, stormed the coach and smashed windows; the sheriff locked him in the closet and hurried him into the Blair jail ahead of the crowd.

framing.detail: The wire headline called him a 'Villain' and treated the crowd as a threat narrowly evaded, without criticism of it.
The Omaha Bee mocked Peppercorn as a 'Lothario' who 'came near stretching hemp' and described him as pale and trembling, with no comment on the crowd.

versions.value: A large crowd gave him a 'warm reception' and made threats of lynching
A crowd assembled but no demonstrations were made at Calhoun
A mob stormed the coach and smashed the windows

conflicts.note: The Omaha Bee relied on dispatches from Blair; the Wheeling item carries a Calhoun dateline of Oct. 25, two days after the event. None is clearly better evidence.

versions.value: Lodged in the Blair jail unharmed and still held in November and December

conflicts.note: The on-demand OCR re-read of the Wheeling item ends with him found dead; the LoC page text of the same article instead ends 'Pepperkorn was hurried into the jail at Blsir ahead of the excited crowd. Trouble is in store for him yet,' so the death is an OCR artifact, not a competing report.

record_check.dossier: Not stated; he is described as a German music teacher whose father held office in Germany, so nothing marks this as anti-Black violence.
One person: Emil Peppercorn (wire copies print Pepperkorn and Pepperkom).
Threats and a rush on the jail; only the Wheeling dispatch describes an assault on the coach, and the Omaha Bee denies any demonstration at Calhoun.
In the sheriff's custody throughout; not taken.
The accounts conflict over what happened at Calhoun.

info: Monday, October 23, 1882, on the afternoon train from Omaha to Blair
The depot at Calhoun (Fort Calhoun), as the train passed, and the depot and jail at Blair
Emil Peppercorn (also Pepperkorn, Pepperkom), a German music teacher; no report gives his race, and one says his father was a public official in Germany
Accused of eloping from Calhoun with his pupil May Frahm, aged 14, and of 'betraying' her; her father also said he had deserted his wife
A 'large crowd' at Calhoun, 'principally Germans' according to the Omaha Bee, and a large crowd at Blair; names not reported
Lodged in the Blair jail unharmed; still held there in November
